opening_summary: Nineteen terms for steering the player, keeping a game fair and setting its rhythm, from communication and anticipation to pacing and spacing. The exact term turns a vague complaint about a level into an instruction you can act on.
opening_description: 19 terms for guiding players and setting the pace.

idea.narration: Hallo. This is Liam, in for Bear. Newcomers often say that good pacing means the challenge keeps rising. That rise is progression. Pacing is the swing between intense and calm moments, a hard fight and then a rest. A straight climb wears the player out. This film goes through the terms of guidance, fairness and rhythm, each one shown, so you can name the exact one.
idea.text:
Good pacing means
the challenge keeps rising.

beats.narration: This table is the map. Nineteen terms about game design, in four groups. The first group is the foundation, with the three pillars, player purpose and communication. It covers what a game needs before anything else.

The second group is guiding the player. Guiding the focus, linear and nonlinear, side quest, level design, teaching through levels, and design the middle first. These terms say how a player finds the way and learns the skills.
The third group is meeting expectations. Anticipation, build-up, logical events, consistent rules, and games can cheat. These terms say whether what happens in a game feels fair, sensible and earned.
The fourth group is rhythm and space. Dynamic, progression, pacing, waves and spacing. These terms say how much happens, how fast it happens, and where.

This drawing is a building on three columns, and the first column, Player, has risen in red. The Three pillars are what a game rests on, the player's role, communication and appeal. The first is Player purpose, what the player does and why. The player, not the game, pushes things forward. For example, in a platformer like Walker the purpose is to reach the goal flag, and every jump is the player's own choice.

The second pillar, Communication, now stands. Without it the player does not know the goal or how to reach it, and feels powerless. The box at the bottom sets it against player purpose. Purpose is what you do and why, and communication is showing you what and how. For example, a goal flag that waves at the far end of the first screen, with a row of coins arching over the first gap, shows a new player both.

The third pillar, Appeal, rises in red, and the roof, the game itself, rests on all three. Appeal is the pull to keep playing. It is the hardest of the three to guarantee, and the most important. For example, if your playtesters finish the first level and ask to play it again, it has appeal. If they put the controller down halfway, it may not.

A room seen from above, with a plain door on the far right. Communication means showing the player the goal and how to reach it, with clues in the space itself. Here nothing marks the door. In this simulated run the player wanders at random and needs two thousand four hundred seventy-six steps to find it. For example, a level that shows its goal flag on the first screen, with a trail of coins pointing the way, communicates the goal.

Now the door is lit in red, with a ring of light around it. Guiding the focus means making clear what the player should concentrate on right now. The same simulated player walks straight there in forty-three steps. Communication tells the player the goal, and guiding the focus tells them where to look now. For example, when a new enemy drops into the level, the camera can pan to it for a moment, so the player looks at the threat.

A chain of rooms, from start to end. Linear and nonlinear describe the route through a level. Linear means one route from start to end, each room opening onto the next. Here there is exactly one route. A linear level is easy to guide, and the designer controls the pace. For example, a tutorial level where the player can only run right, from the first platform to the goal flag, is linear.

Now the chain has two forks. Nonlinear means the player chooses between routes. Each fork offers two ways through, so two times two gives four routes from start to end. For example, a level where the player picks a high path over the rooftops or a low path through the sewer, and later picks again between a ladder and a lift, is nonlinear.

Back to one main line, with one red room off to the side. A Side quest is a detour from the main storyline. It leaves the main line and returns to the same place, so the main story still holds. That gives two ways to finish, with the detour or without it. For example, a cave off the main path, where the player can rescue a lost miner for a reward and then return to the road, is a side quest.

A red staircase climbs as the player learns skills along a famous first level, World one-one. Level design is planning and building the spaces the player moves through. Teaching through levels means the first level lets the player try each skill, with no text. Here seven skills are taught with no tutorial words. For example, level design places the floor, spikes and goal flag of a Walker level, and a level can teach by setting a small, harmless gap before the first deadly one.

A strip of three parts, start, middle and end, with two orders under them. Design the middle first means building the engaging middle levels first, then the opening levels that take players there. The start is played first, but the middle, the red circle, is designed first. For example, you might build the hardest platform room of your game first, note which jumps it demands, then design the opening level to teach exactly those jumps.

Two timelines of an enemy attack, one with no warning and one with a grey wind-up before the red hit. Anticipation means preparing the player for what comes next. In this made-up example, with an assumed reaction time of a quarter of a second, a half-second wind-up leaves a quarter of a second to spare. No wind-up leaves none, and the hit feels cheap. For example, an enemy that crouches and flashes before it lunges gives the player anticipation.
figures: time to spare after reacting: 0.25 s

beats.narration: Three curves rise over the ten seconds before an explosion, sound, sparks, and in red the camera shake. Build-up is a sequence that raises tension toward an event. Anticipation is a short warning before one hit, and build-up is a long rise. In these made-up curves the shake arrives last. For example, before a boss bursts through a wall, the music swells, dust falls from the ceiling and the camera starts to tremble.

A table of player actions and what happens next, with ticks and crosses. Logical events means that what happens makes sense and meets the player's unspoken expectations. Shoot a wall and a bullet hole appears. Walk on gravel and it crunches. In this made-up table, two of the four outcomes meet the expectation. For example, when the player's character lands in water, a splash sound and ripples should follow. A silent landing breaks the expectation.

Two rows of bars show how high a ball bounces, as a percent of the drop. Consistent rules means that even where a game bends physics, it bends it the same way every time. In this made-up example the dark row keeps eighty percent each time, one hundred, eighty, sixty-four and so on. The red row is random, with no rule to learn. For example, if your game gives the player a double jump, it should reach the same height on every level.

A guard seen from above, with a red cone where it looks, and the player sneaking up behind. Games can cheat means hidden help the player does not notice. First, the honest version. In this simulation an honest guard senses all around it, turns at one hundred twenty pixels, and the sneak fails. For example, a platformer that still lets the player jump for a split second after running off a ledge is cheating, and most players never notice.

Now the guard is told not to turn. The player walks right up behind it, and the game lets the ambush happen. That is the cheat, an enemy ignoring what it could sense, so the player's clever play is rewarded. It works only as long as the player does not notice. For example, the script of a patrolling enemy in a stealth level can skip its turn-around whenever the player is right behind it.

A timeline of four team actions in one round, throw smoke, flank, charge in and check angles, all overlapping. Dynamic means many things happening at once, so play stays fresh. Here up to four things happen at the same moment, and the defenders must watch everything. For example, a boss fight where the boss swings at the player while small enemies drop in and the floor starts to crumble is dynamic.

The same four actions, now one after another. The round grows to eighteen seconds, and never more than one thing happens at a time. That is sequential play, the look-alike of dynamic. It is easy to predict, and dull. For example, a boss that only swings, then only summons, then only shakes the floor, each in turn, gives the player one thing to watch at a time.

A line of intensity climbs across four minutes, past a grey comfortable band. Progression is the natural rise in challenge through a game. It should neither over-stimulate nor under-stimulate the player. In these made-up curves a straight climb stays in the band only fifty-six percent of the time, and passes zero point eight near the end. For example, a run of levels where each one adds a faster enemy, a wider gap or a new hazard has progression.

Now the line swings up and down, while its peaks still rise. Pacing means alternating intense and calm moments. In this made-up curve the player stays in the band eighty-eight percent of the time. Pacing is the swing between calm and intense, and progression is the overall rise. For example, a platformer level can follow a tight run of spikes with a quiet stretch and a checkpoint, before the next hard jump.

Two rows of enemy squares, each one wave of total strength ten. Waves means a group of enemies sent together, many weak ones or a few strong ones. Ten enemies of strength one and two enemies of strength five add up to the same total, but the pressure feels different. For example, a tower defence level might send a swarm of small beetles in one wave, then two armoured beetles in the next.

A wide room seen from above, with three characters drifting around it. Spacing means how open or tight the spaces of a level are, open areas to admire, or tight ones that feel claustrophobic, with room left for enemies to move. In this simulated run each character gets seven square metres, and they touch in only seventeen of three hundred frames. For example, a wide cave with a view of a distant castle invites the player to stop and look.

The same length of room, now one metre tall. Each character gets about two point three square metres, and in this simulated run they touch in seventy-two of three hundred frames. Tight space is crowded, tense and claustrophobic, and it changes the pace. For example, a narrow corridor where the player must slip past a patrolling enemy feels tense, and the enemy needs room in it to turn around.
Each pair sets two look-alike terms side by side. Linear means one route from start to end, the rooms in a row on the left. Nonlinear means alternate routes the player picks, the fork on the right.
Anticipation is a short warning just before an event, the grey bar before the red hit. Build-up is a rise in tension toward the event, the long red curve. One is a moment, the other a sequence.
Progression is the overall rise in challenge, the straight line on the left. Pacing is the swing between calm and intense, the wavy line on the right, which still rises as it swings.

Logical events means things behave sensibly, so a shot wall gets a bullet hole. Consistent rules means bent physics is bent the same way every time. The dark bars shrink by a rule, and the red ones jump around.

A vague request sits above the exact instruction that replaces it. Players keep getting lost becomes, light the exit door and put a ring of light around it, visible from the start. In the simulated run, steps to the door fall from two thousand four hundred seventy-six to forty-three.

The enemy hits feel cheap becomes, add a half-second wind-up animation before every attack. With an assumed reaction time of a quarter of a second, no wind-up leaves no time, and the wind-up leaves a quarter of a second to spare.
The level feels flat becomes, alternate sixty seconds of enemies with thirty seconds of calm, and send the strongest wave last. The chart shows peaks and rests that keep rising overall.
The ending is a letdown becomes, build up for ten seconds, with sound rising, sparks flying and the camera shaking before the blast. The curve climbs slowly, then steeply.

The physics feel random becomes, bounces keep eighty percent of the height every time. One hundred, eighty, sixty-four, and down. Each bounce is eighty percent of the last, a rule the player can learn.
This is a checklist of six questions to ask before you call the pacing done. First, does the player know their role, the goal, and how to reach it? That is player purpose and communication.
Second, can the player tell where to look, and do they have alternatives? That is guiding the focus, and a nonlinear route or a side quest.
Third, is every danger telegraphed, shown before it strikes, as anticipation asks? And do events behave as the player expects, as logical events should?
Fourth, are the rules consistent, bent the same way every time? And if the game cheats, is the cheat hidden, and does it help the player?
Fifth, does the pace alternate and still rise, inside a comfortable band? That is pacing and progression working together, calm and intense in turn on a line that keeps rising.
Sixth, is there room to move, or is the space tight on purpose? Then say it exactly. Not the level feels flat, but sixty seconds of enemies, thirty seconds of calm.

recap_lines: A game rests on three pillars, the player, communication and appeal.
Communication shows the goal, and guiding the focus shows where to look now.
Linear has one route, and nonlinear lets the player choose between routes.
Anticipation is a short warning, and build-up is a long rise in tension.
Consistent rules bend physics the same way every time.
Progression is the overall rise, and pacing swings between calm and intense.

your_turn.command: Quiz me on game design terms with short cases from making a platformer, one at a time. Use the terms communication, guiding the focus, linear, nonlinear, side quest, anticipation, build-up, consistent rules, progression and pacing. For each case I must name the exact term and say why its look-alike is wrong. Hold back the answer until I reply, then tell me if I was right.
checks: Check: each case is a game-making situation, and the answer waits for you.
Check: you named the exact term and said why its look-alike is wrong.

deck_problems: Slide 9 (Dynamic play), step 1: the caption says 'Total time 8 s', but the string is hard-coded. The four actions (durations 3, 5, 3 and 7 s, starting at 0, 1, 2 and 0, as the note says) all end by 7 s, and the bars stop at 7 on an 8-second axis. It should say 7 s. The narration does not speak the total.

Slide 1 says '19 terms from three video lectures on game design', but the slides cite two videos (the tips video and Crash Course 'Game Design') plus the course glossary, and the title slide's note says the terms come from the tips video and the Crash Course lecture.

'Dynamic' is defined two ways in the course. The deck says 'Many things happening at once, so play stays fresh'. GLOSSARY-jargon-midterm.md (Game design documents) defines Dynamic as 'Behaviour that emerges when mechanics interact'. The slide does not say that the glossary uses the word differently.

'Spacing' also has two meanings in course material. The deck uses it for open against tight level spaces. RIOT-SERIES-TERMS.md (6.12) defines Spacing as how far an object moves between animation frames. 'Anticipation' is consistent between the two.

Slide 8 (Games can cheat), step 2: the caption 'ambush: the guard never turned' can never appear. The player stops at 80 px from the guard, and that caption needs under 60 px, so the step ends on 'sneaking up from behind' and the ambush is never shown.

Slide 10: the badge says Computed, but the note says the intensity curves are illustrative (only time in the band is computed from them). Slide 13 is also badged Computed over an assumed reaction time and illustrative curves. On slide 10 step 2 the paced curve dips below the band at the start, while the caption says peaks then rests keep the player in the band.
Slide 10 step 2 note: 'The tower defence game alternates waves...' uses a definite article for a game that is never named or introduced.

Slide 13 step 4: 'intensity at 90% of the way: 0.77' comes from a single curve (x to the power 2.5) that appears nowhere else; slide 6 shows the same build-up as three curves with sound 0.85, sparks 0.81, shake 0.73 at 90%.

Slide 13 step 3: the instruction is '60 s of enemies, 30 s of calm, strongest wave last', but the chart is slide 10's sine curve, with equal high and low halves and four peaks, so it does not show the two-to-one timing or a strongest last wave.
Slide 5 step 1: the labels 'move right' and 'jump' overlap each other and the red line, and 'blocks' and 'pit' sit on the line.

Slide 3: one picture (the lit door) serves both Communication and Guiding the focus, so the picture cannot show the difference the TELL THESE APART box asks for. In step 1 the door is already drawn and visible, only unlit, so 'Nothing says where the goal is' is not quite what is shown.
Slide 7 step 1: '2 of 4 events meet the expectation' counts a right and a wrong version of the same two events, so the fraction is built into the table rather than found.

Slide 14 item 3 uses 'telegraphed', a word no slide defines. Slide 2's TELL THESE APART box sets Player purpose against Communication before Communication's entry appears (slide 3), and slide 3 step 1 shows the Guiding the focus box before its entry appears.
GAME-DESIGN-TERMS-source-crashcourse.md lists 'goals versus tactics' among deck C's terms, but the deck has no such term; its 19 terms match the map without it.
